notes.note: كُنْتُ تَعْبَانَ uses the colloquial adjective تَعْبَان; the course's own MSA word for 'tired' is مُتْعَب (day46 newWords 'mutab', مَا زِلْتُ مُتْعَبًا). Consider كُنْتُ مُتْعَبًا in both places for consistency (register, not an error).
لَازِم أَنْ is everyday rather than formal MSA (the intro acknowledges يَجِبُ as 'more formal'). Acceptable as polite spoken MSA; an alternative formal pattern is مِنَ اللَّازِمِ أَنْ or يَجِبُ أَنْ.
عَلَى ظَهْرَيْهِمَا (dual) is understandable; classical style prefers the plural for a pair of single body parts belonging to two people: عَلَى ظُهُورِهِمَا. Style only.

the wrong form ثَلَاثَة مَرَّات and the right form ثَلَاثَ مَرَّات both transliterate as 'Thalātha marrāt', so the learner cannot hear the difference the mistake is about. In connected speech the construct ة would be thalāthat(u) marrāt; consider showing 'thalāthat marrāt' for the wrong form or vocalising it ثَلَاثَةُ.

ثَمَانٍ وَثَلَاثُونَ دَرَجَة: the counted noun after 11-99 is accusative singular (دَرَجَةً); the course omits most final vowels on nouns, so this is house style, but دَرَجَةً would model the rule if the owner vocalises it anywhere.

English adds 'all day' ('I'll be busy all day on Saturday'); the Arabic سَأَكُونُ مَشْغُولًا يَوْمَ السَّبْت just says 'I'll be busy on Saturday'. Harmless, but the literal learner may look for a word for 'all day'.
English 'See you on Sunday!' for إِلَى اللِّقَاء ('see you / until we meet'); 'on Sunday' is not in the Arabic.
the tap gloss for يَد reads "hand ('hand luggage')" — a mnemonic from another lesson appearing as the dictionary meaning; 'hand' alone is clearer.
the tap for لَا in prohibitions (لَا تَشْرَبْ, لَا تَنْسَ) shows 'no'; the segs in the same lesson say 'don't'. A context-sensitive 'don't (before an order)' would match the segs.

لِلْمُبَارَاة / الْمُبَارَاة are rendered 'li-l-mubārāh' / 'al-mubārāh' (ة after ā as -h). This is the ALA-LC convention, so not an error, but it is the only place in the chunk where ة appears as 'h' and may puzzle a learner who sees 'qiṣṣa', 'ḥarāra' elsewhere.

summary: Read the whole export for days 41-50 (2,733 lines: titles, intros, objectives, sentences with mistakes, dialogues, readings, quizzes, completions) and checked every Arabic string for spelling, harakat, case, agreement and verb mood (لَمْ jussive, أَنْ subjunctive, imperatives, prohibitions, faʿlān feminines, compound numbers), the English and literal translations, every seg and tap gloss, every answer key and the transliteration. The Arabic itself is clean: I found no misspelt word, wrong case ending, agreement error, wrong verb form or wrong answer key in the ten days. All 14 errors are in the gloss/transliteration layer: 3 major tap glosses that teach the wrong meaning (سَلَامَتُكِ labelled 'to a man' in day43 and day46, تَفْتَحُ glossed as passive 'is opened' in day44, negative مَا glossed 'what' in day41), 8 minor glosses where a dictionary entry does not fit the sentence it is tapped in (imperatives glossed as 3rd-person present, 'after an'/'after lam' labels on the wrong forms, فِي الْيَوْم 'today', vocalised أَنْتِ described as unvocalised), 1 minor grammar-fact (day41 culture gives colloquial salāmtik for the feminine, contradicting day43), and 3 engine issues (bare ة transliterated as 'A / at', proclitic+name capitalised as one word 'Wasāmī', شَاي as 'Shāī'). The recurring pattern is that tap glosses come from a single dictionary sense and are reused in sentences where another sense or form is meant, and that the dictionary glosses of the 'wrong' forms in mistakes blocks were copied from the 'right' forms. Notes cover register (تَعْبَان, لَازِم), two small additions in English translations, and transliteration limits that hide a contrast (ثَلَاثَة vs ثَلَاثَ).
